Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
News reports about events similar to what happened to me
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: The people responsible have faced no consequences
I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of witnessed other trauma, the appraisal that others can see what happened to me by looking at me is hard to reconcile unless there was also direct victimization or visible injury. The rest of the profile centers on witnessing, guilt about failing to protect, and anger that perpetrators were not held accountable, which fits. This item implies a conspicuous personal mark or shame signal not otherwise supported by the triggers, memory, or strategies, so it is clinically incoherent within this profile.

vignette: Seventy-year-old Elena Hernandez, a renowned fashion designer, sat in her spacious studio, surrounded by vibrant fabrics and half-finished garments. Her eyes wandered to a photo of her late niece, Sophia, who had been killed in a devastating earthquake three years ago. The memory still felt like an open wound. Elena recalled the day she witnessed the destruction on live television - the screams, the crumbling buildings, and the desperate pleas for help. She had been powerless to stop it. As the anniversary of the earthquake approached, Elena found herself becoming increasingly irritable and withdrawn. Certain triggers set her off: a specific temperature on her skin, like the warmth of that fateful day, made her feel uneasy; news reports about similar disasters transported her back to the chaos; and any loss of control, no matter how minor, sent her spiraling into anxiety. To cope with these triggers, Elena began avoiding anything that reminded her of Sophia - photos, mementos, even conversations about her niece's favorite hobbies. She stopped watching the news, fearful of being confronted with images or stories that would unleash a torrent of emotions. These avoidance strategies seemed to provide temporary relief, but they also left Elena feeling disconnected from her loved ones and her own creative pursuits. Her designs, once a reflection of her vibrant personality, now felt dull and uninspired. The memory of the earthquake continued to haunt her, forcing its way into her mind when she least expected it. Full sensory reliving was a regular occurrence - the sounds, smells, and sights all came flooding back without warning. Elena couldn't shake off the feeling that she should have done more to protect Sophia, that her own actions (or lack thereof) had contributed to the tragedy. She became consumed by self-blame, wondering if there had been something she could have done differently. The fact that no one was held accountable for the disaster only fueled her anger and frustration. These negative appraisals fed into the memory of the earthquake, making it even more vivid and distressing. As Elena struggled to come to terms with her emotions, she began pushing away positive feelings - laughter, joy, even love - because they felt unsafe. She couldn't bear the thought of letting her guard down, only to be blindsided by another tragedy. Her relationships suffered as a result; her husband, once her rock, now felt like a stranger. The cycle was suffocating: triggers led to avoidance strategies, which in turn fueled negative appraisals and intrusive memories. Elena's world had shrunk to the point where she could barely leave her studio without being overwhelmed by anxiety. The weight of her grief, combined with the pressure to maintain a façade of strength, finally broke her. She realized that she needed help to break free from this self-reinforcing cycle. Elena's eyes drifted back to Sophia's photo, and for a moment, she allowed herself to feel the pain. It was a small step towards confronting her demons, but it was enough to bring her to seek professional help. With trepidation, Elena picked up the phone, hoping that therapy would provide her with the tools to heal and find a way back to living, rather than just existing.
